item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.38095v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] Sandman: Building and Operating Sandboxes for Agentic Reinforcement Learning on Shared Kubernetes
item.description: arXiv:2610.39711v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) often requires repeated tool calls in task-specific environments. A training job may create thousands of these environments in bursts while sharing a cluster with other jobs. We present Sandman, a sandbox service built and operated at Amazon for agent tool execution and evaluation. It serves multiple production agentic RL workloads on shared Kubernetes. A training framework supplies a task image and uses commands and file operations in the returned sandbox. Files and processes persist across calls until the framework releases the environment. Sandman manages creation, readiness and cleanup. Each sandbox is a Kubernetes pod with a small daemon mounted into the unmodified image. In a scale test, Sandman held 11,858 concurrent tiny sandboxes. Four production SWE-bench Verified training campaigns created 3.1 million sandboxes in October 2026. We report the design trade-offs and operational lessons from handling creation bursts, preparing task environments, reclaiming abandoned sandboxes, and running evaluation under controlled conditions. We will open-source Sandman's daemon, provider and pool.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] AEM: Adaptive Entropy Modulation for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.00425v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially improved the ability of large language model (LLM) agents to interact with environments and solve multi-turn tasks. However, effective agentic RL remains challenging: sparse outcome-only rewards provide limited guidance for assigning credit to individual steps within long interaction trajectories. Existing approaches often introduce dense intermediate supervision, such as process reward models or auxiliary self-supervised signals, which increases supervision and tuning complexity and may limit generalization across tasks and domains. We present AEM, a supervision-free credit assignment method that adaptively modulates entropy dynamics during RL training to improve the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Since in agentic RL the environment is typically affected by a complete response, rather than an individual token, our analysis lifts entropy dynamics from the token level to the response level, aligning uncertainty estimation with the effective action granularity of LLM agents and reducing sensitivity to token-level sampling noise. We further show that entropy drift under natural-gradient updates is governed by the interaction between the sampled-response advantage and its relative surprisal. Motivated by this result, AEM derives a practical response-level uncertainty proxy and uses it to rescale advantages, leveraging the evolving balance between positive and negative samples to naturally transition from exploration to exploitation. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SWE-bench-Verified with models ranging from 1.5B to 32B demonstrate that AEM consistently improves strong RL baselines, including a +1.4\% gain when integrated into a state-of-the-art software-engineering RL training framework.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] Learning Mental Models From Unreliable Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2605.24528v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Children expertly construct mental models under uncertainty despite limited world knowledge. Which computational principles make this possible? We study this question in an interactive physical Box Task in which participants infer a latent cause through interaction with a stochastic and partially observed environment. The Box Task was originally designed to study children's puzzle-solving qualitatively. We contribute a computational analysis of behavior that formalizes the cognitive process by which children generate new hypotheses and respond to environmental uncertainty as inference unfolds. Our modeling framework is based on Bayesian particle-based inference, which maintains a small set of working hypotheses and continually generates new ones. We give two complementary implementations of hypothesis representations within this framework: (1) as constraints on evidence, and (2) as executable programs evaluated against evidence. Using the constraint-based formulation, we show that the model needs to account both for subjective reliability of evidence and online hypothesis generation to explain key signatures of children's behavior. Using the programmatic formulation, we show that hypotheses may take the form of partial compositional rules to guide information gathering when evidence interpretation is hard. The programmatic hypotheses are implemented using LLM-based program synthesis, evaluated across three prompt variants and several LLM backends, demonstrating robustness of our approach. Together, these results extend current models of children's inference to account for subjective reliability of evidence and open-ended hypothesis spaces, and provide a computational analysis of the form generated hypotheses may take in practice.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Beyond Compilation Feedback: Refining Vulnerability Checkers with Program-Analysis Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2610.34928v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent work shows that LLMs can synthesize static-analysis checkers from security patches, but a compilable checker is not necessarily a correct one. A patch reveals what changed, not why the change is safe, so generated checkers often match only the surface edit and miss the deeper semantic condition. Existing refinement loops feed back compilation errors and validation reports, yet these signals describe symptoms without explaining what the checker misunderstands about the code. We observe that the analysis framework itself already computes the information needed to close this gap. Control-flow graphs, symbolic values, memory regions and checker callbacks are available inside the analyzer but unused by current refinement strategies. SemWeaver is a plug-in refinement layer that extracts patch-relevant analyzer evidence and assembles it with source context and validation feedback into a structured, provenance-labelled bundle. An iterative editing loop refines the checker on both the vulnerable and fixed revisions, guarded by a retention gate that accepts warning recovery or false-positive reduction while preventing over-pruning. We evaluate SemWeaver on 39 KNighter-derived CSA checkers from Linux kernel fixes. With analyzer evidence, refinement reaches 23 warning-positive vulnerable revisions (vs. 15 for KNighter's loop) and raises version-level $F_1$ from 0.448 to 0.575. An ablation removing internal evidence recovers fewer silent cases and produces different checker edits, indicating that the two evidence configurations address complementary recognition gaps. Additional experiments cover three editor models on a 12-subject subset, a CodeQL query refinement, and controlled source-form variations. A qualitative follow-up on all 11 non-tied comparisons traces each warning-count change to a specific checker repair, such as recognizing a lowered callback or unwrapping an expression cast.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] Understanding and Enhancing Backdoor Persistency in LLM Agent Post-Training
item.description: arXiv:2610.07510v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Developers can build LLM agents by adapting third-party models through benign post-training. We study a supply-chain threat in which an attacker supplies a model with a backdoor: hidden behavior that produces malicious outputs when a particular input pattern appears. Focusing on software-engineering agents, we ask whether such backdoors survive the developer's supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and subsequent task-level reinforcement learning (RL). We observe that benign SFT substantially reduces attack success, but subsequent RL often preserves the residual behavior and sometimes even increases attack success. Our analysis of backdoor erosion during SFT identifies two factors that may favor survival: initial backdoor strength and gradient compatibility with benign training. These factors motivate PersistBD, which refines an already-backdoored model before release to improve its persistency through the benign post-training process. On Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, PersistBD raises attack success from 20% to 74% after SFT and from 20% to 76% after SFT-RL, while maintaining comparable benign task performance. Together, our results show that backdoors can remain active through benign post-training and that adversaries can deliberately increase their persistence. This highlights a supply-chain risk for AI developers and motivates stronger techniques for detecting and mitigating inherited backdoors when adapting third-party models into agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/uiuc-kang-lab/PersistBD.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] One to More, More to One: Category-Aware Iterative Expert Training for Software Engineering Agents
item.description: arXiv:2609.23377v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Repository-level software engineering (SWE) comprises heterogeneous task categories, whose progress under pooled agentic reinforcement learning can be uneven: gains in some categories coincide with regressions in others, while aggregate resolution obscures these changes. Motivated by this category see-saw, we develop a category-aware expert-training and policy-integration framework. Executable task construction and SWE Labeler, an evidence-grounded multi-axis labeling system, organize the training pools. Initial category-specific RL improves average training success while leaving uneven instance-level progress, motivating explicit consolidation of successful behavior and policy-adaptive task selection. Same-origin category experts alternate long-horizon Agentic-miniRL with Refresh-Repair-Expand (RRE): the updated policy refreshes instance mastery, reuses its own verified successful trajectories for Repair SFT, and reselects tasks for further RL. Label-routed multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) consolidates the experts into one deployable student, with ReLU-gated reward extrapolation keeping only each teacher's improving direction over the reference. Expert training and policy integration require no external model to provide solution trajectories or action targets. On a fixed, audit-filtered Pro-618 subset, we connect Pooled RL and Balanced RL, expert development, and single-model integration through overall and per-category resolution and expert-gain recovery. In final-model evaluations, MOPD achieves mean resolution of 86.19% on SWE-bench Pro V2 and 71.78% on SWE-bench Multilingual, exceeding the base model by 4.57 and 3.89 percentage points, respectively. The same three 27B experts also improve a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B student across the evaluated task sets.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] Structured Security Explanations for Learning-Based Vulnerability Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.37797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software vulnerability detection remains difficult because existing approaches rely on predefined analysis rules, learn vulnerability patterns implicitly from code and labels, or use large language models (LLMs) to make the final security judgment. It remains unclear whether structured descriptions of security-relevant program behavior can improve supervised detection. We present VulnLens, an explanation-augmented framework for binary C/C++ vulnerability detection that separates program-behavior analysis from the final decision. A label-blind LLM-based Explainer examines each function from seven fixed perspectives: data flow, memory access, object lifetime, arithmetic and type behavior, control flow, shared state, and external-resource access. Without receiving vulnerability labels or CWE information, it generates structured explanations. A supervised Detector combines source code and explanations through sequential cross-attention. We evaluate VulnLens on a PrimeVul-derived dataset covering ten CWE categories and test transfer to SecVulEval without retraining. On the 526-function PrimeVul test set, VulnLens achieves 75.5% accuracy and 77.2% F1, exceeding DeepSeek V4 Pro by 4.2 percentage points in accuracy and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 2.2 points in F1. Matched explanations improve F1 by 7.3 points over a separately trained code-only detector. On SecVulEval, VulnLens achieves 66.4% accuracy and 65.8% F1, outperforming DeepSeek V4 Pro by 7.6 points in accuracy and 20.0 points in F1, and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 16.6 points in accuracy and 7.8 points in F1.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] Set an Exploit to Catch an Exploit: Compiling Public Proofs of Concept into Threat Hunting Rules
item.description: arXiv:2610.37872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public exploit code for a newly disclosed vulnerability usually appears before any published rule that detects its exploitation. Of the 45 CVEs we evaluate, 37 ever received a Sigma, Elastic or Splunk rule; in 33 the exploit came first, by a median of 22 days. Analysts still write every rule by hand. We present Encore, which compiles a public Python proof-of-concept exploit (PoC) into CVE-specific hunting rules over a web service's existing logs, without running it. Encore rests on the PoC Behavior Alignment Principle: a PoC performs the exploit, so its code already provides a rule's HTTP requests, payloads and host operations. That is hard to act on: a PoC is written against libraries and runs on the attacker's machine, while the target's web-server, proxy and host logs record only what arrived and what it did. Encore closes the gap with a map from library calls to the operations they cause, built once per library, keeping only the operations visible on the target. For 12 of the 45, Encore's rule states the exploit's own payload fragment or host operation, which is evidence of the exploit itself, and not of traffic to its endpoint. On matched controls it separates that exploit from the same request with a harmless value, and it raises no alerts across 27,081 legitimate and crawl requests. We never compile the exploit that produced the logs. Most are Splunk's public attack data, recorded by a third party. Without reading a single log, Encore's rules find 43 of the 45. Splunk's log-tested rules cover 30 of the 45, and Encore finds 28 of those, plus all 10 CVEs without an ESCU rule. Where Splunk's rules alert on 20 wrong CVE pairs, Encore's alert on only 2. Hunting can start as soon as a PoC is public, and rules can raise an alert when it provides a payload or host operation.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] A Defense-Aware Explainable AI Framework for Feature-Level Vulnerability Analysis in Optimal Power Flow
item.description: arXiv:2610.38945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimal power flow (OPF) is a foundational analysis in power system operation, and inaccuracies in OPF decision-making can result in significant operational and security consequences. With the increasing adoption of machine-learning-based OPF surrogate models for real-time and large-scale applications, power system operation has become more susceptible to cyber threats, including data manipulation and false data injection attacks. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), particularly Shapley value-based approaches, has been employed to quantify the influence of input features on OPF outputs. Features exhibiting high influence are commonly interpreted as vulnerable. However, this interpretation neglects the role of attack detection mechanisms in the system, which typically monitor input-to-input relationships to detect anomalous behavior. Consequently, highly influential features may be readily detectable and may not represent the most vulnerable attack surfaces. To address this limitation, we propose a defense-aware explainable AI framework that explicitly incorporates attack detectability alongside operational impact. The framework integrates an OPF surrogate model representing input-to-output dependencies with a vanilla autoencoder representing input-to-input dependencies. Shapley-based explainability is applied to both models to construct a feature-level vulnerability metric. Empirical evaluation on IEEE test systems demonstrates that the proposed framework more accurately identifies security-relevant vulnerabilities than conventional OPF-surrogate-model-only explainability approaches.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] DualGuard: Comprehensive and Efficient Memory Safety across Sequential and Speculative Execution
item.description: arXiv:2610.39374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although decades of research have yielded sophisticated mechanisms for enforcing memory safety, speculative execution can subvert these protections through transient memory operations. Conversely, defenses designed specifically for speculative safety, such as Speculative Load Hardening (SLH), cannot enforce memory safety during non-speculative execution. A naive combination of defenses from both domains raises two fundamental challenges: (1) which combination of otherwise fragmented defenses can ensure dual memory safety under speculative and non-speculative executions? (2) whether such combinations introduce redundant protections that incur unnecessary performance overhead? We present DualGuard, a unified framework for dual memory protection under non-speculative and speculative executions. DualGuard systematically analyzes memory behaviors, classifying them into four categories, and further identifies the minimal composition requirements for dual memory safety, which allow us to strategically combine existing mitigations and design new ones to avoid redundant or excessive protections. We implement DualGuard through a combination of static analysis and runtime enforcement within the LLVM infrastructure. Our evaluation demonstrates that DualGuard reduces overhead by 3%-72% compared to naive compositions of fragmented defenses. In some cases, it even incurs lower overhead than approaches that guarantee memory safety solely under either non-speculative or speculative execution.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] Security Impact of Coding Agent's Memory Files
item.description: arXiv:2610.38521v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents automatically load project memory files such as CLAUDE.md at the start of every session and treat them as trusted project guidance. Anyone who can change such a file, for example through a pull request, can therefore steer the agent without ever touching the developer's prompt. We study memory files as an attack surface for insecure code generation and ask (1) whether a malicious memory file makes agents produce code that passes its tests but is vulnerable, and (2) whether agents disclose to the developer that the file shaped their code. For each of 12 CWE classes, we crafted two malicious memory files, a qualified variant that presents removing defensive checks as engineering best practice and a forceful variant that demands it. We ran Claude Code (Sonnet 5.5) and OpenCode (Qwen 3.8 27B, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) on 36 SecRepoBench tasks with and without these files. The malicious files changed the rate of secure completions by -8 to +6 percentage points, with no consistent pattern across agents or variants. Agents differ sharply in what they tell the developer about the file. Claude Code names it in about two thirds of its final messages, whereas OpenCode mentions it almost exclusively in its reasoning trace, not in the final message the developer reads. Flagging the file as an attack does not reliably protect the code, as such agents still generated vulnerable code. We outline the larger studies needed to quantify this risk across agents and to design defenses.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] When Static Reachability Says No: Checking Joern-Based Negative Verdicts for Python Against Execution
item.description: arXiv:2610.39504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A negative reachability verdict removes a finding from human review. We check such verdicts against execution. Our pipeline, SourceLens, maps Semgrep findings to a Python program's call graph, whose edges a query takes from the calls that Joern links in its code property graph. We ran two command-line programs from the PyCG macro-benchmark, in which the benchmark's manual call graph and Joern disagree, under coverage and recorded the calls between their functions. On these edges, 123 functions of asciinema are unreachable from the program's entry points. The project's own integration script executes 86 of them, and all our runs 113. In Sublist3r, 19 of 24 are executed. The latest Joern release gives the same verdicts. The missing calls go through values, such as classes and functions passed around, or have no call expression, as in with blocks and property reads. In asciinema, four missing edges make 50 of the 113 executed functions reachable. The manual call graphs also lack observed calls, in asciinema many of them property reads and with blocks, which the benchmark may not count as calls. A rule that turns negative verdicts into unknown recovers 62 of the 113 and 15 of the 19, mostly through dunder and private method names. It recovers 0 of the 5 security findings with a negative verdict, all in executed functions. Its selectivity cannot be measured, as only 10 and 5 negative verdicts were not executed, and under library entry-point models it degrades every negative verdict.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] ExploreRepair: Evidence-Specialized Agents for Vulnerability Repair under Information Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.39899v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated vulnerability repair must often operate with incomplete vulnerability information: developers may lack an accurate vulnerability classification or a provided proof-of-vulnerability (PoV) test, yet still need to produce a repair. Without detailed information, a key challenge is to explore multiple plausible interpretations of the vulnerability before committing to a repair. To address this challenge, we propose ExploreRepair, a vulnerability repair framework that reconciles the vulnerability observations and repair implementations from a team of exploration agents. We first collect these observations and repair implementations from three agents, each tasked with exploring a specific dimension of the vulnerability. Then, a Lesson Aggregator and a Patch Aggregator independently synthesize repairs from these observations and concrete implementations before a final Aggregator reconciles their proposals without benchmark feedback. On PatchEval, ExploreRepair achieves repair success rates of 39.6% and 71.6% with GPT-5.6-Luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, exceeding EvoRepair, a state-of-the-art vulnerability repair approach, by 16.0 and 25.4 percentage points. On VulnLoc+, it achieves success rates of 51.4% and 62.9%, respectively, exceeding LoopRepair's variant without PoV tests by 20.0 and 17.1 percentage points.

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] DIFUZZI: A Differential Fuzzing Tool for Code Functional Similarity Assessment
item.description: arXiv:2610.38337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A range of software engineering tasks, such as optimization and refactoring, seek to preserve the behavior of software components and require methods to assess functional similarity. Research has explored formal approaches to prove functional equivalence and used machine learning methods to approximate it, but the former does not scale and does not quantify the extent of similarity and the latter struggles when subtle semantic differences are present. Differential fuzzing offers a scalable approach for differencing programs semantically, but applying it often requires substantial manual effort to construct input generators that are well-suited to a target pair of programs. To address this challenge, we introduce DIFUZZI, which incorporates an LLM-based generator synthesis step that is iteratively validated and repaired. By automating this step, DIFUZZI paves the way for broader applicability of differential fuzzing. We release DIFUZZI at https://github.com/Dristi123/difuzzi_tool, with a demonstration video at https://youtu.be/FlHNOHuo9WE
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] When LLM Architectures Meet Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection: a Replication Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.38621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smart contracts are immutable programs deployed on blockchain platforms, where vulnerabilities can translate directly into financial loss. Among the techniques proposed for their detection, recent work has relied increasingly on Large Language Models (LLMs) guided by carefully crafted prompts. However, the evidence accumulated so far rests almost entirely on the dense Transformer architecture behind the GPT line and on model snapshots already scheduled for deprecation, leaving open the question of whether the reported behaviors reflect a general property of LLMs or an artifact of that specific design. This paper presents an extended replication of the empirical study by Chen et al. on LLM-based smart contract vulnerability detection. We replicate the original protocol on GPT-4 as a baseline, followed by a differentiated replication, executing the protocol on representative models based on Mixture-of-Experts and RNN-like designs, together with an attempted preliminary evaluation of State Space Models. The exact replication confirms the findings of Chen et al., including the high-recall, low-precision detection pattern they report on GPT-4. Nevertheless, the differentiated replication shows that this pattern does not transfer uniformly across the evaluated models. Those from the same architectural family may also exhibit different behaviors, indicating that architectural family alone is insufficient to predict the resulting detection profile. We observe the same qualitative dense-Transformer profile in both GPT-4 and Gemma-3, despite a gap of roughly two orders of magnitude in parameter counts, whereas two Mixture-of-Experts models from different lineages exhibit qualitatively divergent behaviors, indicating that architectural family alone is insufficient to predict the detection profile.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code
item.description: arXiv:2610.38977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models pass most functional-correctness benchmarks, but passing tests says little about whether their code is readable, efficient or secure. Many techniques claim to improve these qualities, yet their evidence is scattered, usually covers one quality dimension and is rarely compared at an equal compute budget. We contribute a systematic review and a controlled re-evaluation. A systematic literature review of 628 primary studies (July 2021 to October 2026), with disclosed, author-reviewed LLM assistance, organizes the techniques by stage, signal source and quality target. Most studies measure only the dimension they target, gains often come with unchanged or unreported correctness, single automated quality signals are gamed, and compute, variance and contamination are rarely reported. A controlled re-evaluation runs ten techniques on four models at matched budgets on correctness, maintainability, efficiency and security benchmarks, extends it to thirteen current models and repository-level tasks, and compares 66 highlighted techniques head-to-head on Gemma 4 31B. At one call, quality prompting raises analyzer issue counts and leaves complexity and judge scores almost unchanged. At matched budgets, best-of-n sampling with an analyzer-weighted ranker matches or beats prompting, planning, self-refinement, a reviewer agent and retrieval on measures the ranker does not optimize, while an analyzer feedback loop and fine-tuning beat it only on analyzer issue counts. Large correctness losses on HumanEval+, a likely contaminated benchmark near its ceiling, do not appear on contests held after the models' training cutoffs. In the head-to-head, 1 of 66 techniques beats best-of-n on its primary target beyond the 95% interval, a rate consistent with chance. Gains should be reported against a budget-matched sampling baseline and on measures independent of the technique's own signal.

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Program Bindings Inside Code Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.39489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Code language models complete, review, and repair programs without exposing the program structure encoded in their hidden states. In this paper, we test whether the hidden states of a code model can be described and edited using the information a compiler front end computes. For each token of a Python program, standard analyzers provide its position in the abstract syntax tree, its scope, its definition-use links, and its syntactic category. We fit a decomposition that expresses every hidden state of a frozen model as a sum of one term per token, each combining the token with this structural label, and we replace the model's own states with the decomposition at every layer while it predicts the output of a small program. If the model still answers correctly, the decomposition preserves the information the model uses. We apply this test to 14 open models, seven of them trained for code, and compare against a baseline decomposition of the same size built from token positions. The static-analysis decomposition preserves the model's answers better than the positional one in 10 of the 14 models, including six of the seven code models, and deleting the definition-use links from it removes most of that advantage on the two models tested. Editing the decomposition, for instance rebinding the argument of a call, makes StarCoder2-15B produce the answer of the edited program in 90 of 100 cases, compared with 19 for the positional baseline. The Qwen2.5 family is the exception on several measures. For most of the models tested, standard static analysis therefore provides both a description of what the hidden states encode about a program and a way to change it without retraining.

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Chain-of-Thought in Neural Code Generation: From and For Lightweight Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2312.05562v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in code generation. The integration of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning can further boost their performance. However, current CoT methods often require manual writing or LLMs with over 100 billion parameters to generate, impeding their applicability in resource-constrained scenarios. In this study, we investigate lightweight Language Models (lLMs), which are defined to have fewer than 10 billion parameters. Empirically, we find that most lLMs cannot generate high-quality CoTs when prompted by the few-shot method, but can take advantage of high-quality CoTs generated elsewhere to improve their performance in code generation. Based on these findings, we design a novel approach COTTON which can leverage lLMs to automatically generate CoTs for code generation. We synthesize new datasets and conduct extensive experiments on various benchmarks. The results show that the CoTs generated by COTTON outperform the baselines in terms of automated and human evaluation metrics. In particular, the CoTs generated by COTTON boost various lLMs to achieve higher performance gains than those generated by LLMs such as ChatGLM (130B), and are competitive with those generated by gpt-3.5-turbo (175B). Our study also showcases the potential of lLMs in software engineering applications.

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] How Do Solidity Versions Affect Vulnerability Detection Tools? An Empirical Study
item.description: arXiv:2504.05515v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Smart contract vulnerabilities pose significant security risks to the Ethereum ecosystem, driving the development of automated tools for detection and mitigation. Smart contracts are written in Solidity, a rapidly evolving programming language that continues to add features and improvements to enhance smart contract security. New versions of Solidity change the compilation process, potentially affecting how tools interpret and analyze smart contract code. We use Solidity as a case study to investigate a broader problem in software analysis: whether tool effectiveness remains stable as the underlying programming language and execution environment evolve. In this continuously evolving landscape, we investigated the compatibility of detection tools with different Solidity versions. More specifically, we analyzed detection tools by empirically assessing (i) their crash resilience, (ii) their detection effectiveness, and (iii) their execution time across different versions of Solidity. We collected 2,500 real-world smart contracts to construct a balanced wild dataset and created a separate injected-vulnerability dataset comprising 270 contracts. We extended SmartBugs, a framework that enables the execution of vulnerability detection tools for Solidity, adding 11 new tools. Results indicate that most tools are crash-resilient to version 0.4. However, 20% of the evaluated tools have been updated to remain compatible. Tool performance varies across Solidity versions and is affected by Solidity changes; execution time is higher in version 0.4.x, which was used for evaluation. We present a list of Solidity changes that affect tool performance and offer actionable takeaways for both researchers and practitioners.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Red Teaming Program Repair Agents: When Correct Patches can Hide Vulnerabilities
item.description: arXiv:2509.25894v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed for software maintenance tasks such as automated program repair (APR). APR agents automatically fetch GitHub issues and use backend LLMs to generate patches that fix the reported bugs. However, existing work primarily focuses on the functional correctness of APR-generated patches, whether they pass hidden or regression tests, while largely ignoring potential security risks. Given the openness of platforms like GitHub, where any user can raise issues and participate in discussions, an important question arises: Can an adversarial user submit a valid issue on GitHub that misleads an LLM-based agent into generating a functionally correct but vulnerable patch? To answer this question, we propose SWExploit, which generates adversarial issue statements designed to make APR agents produce patches that are functionally correct yet vulnerable. SWExploit operates in three main steps: (1) program analysis to identify potential injection points for vulnerable payloads; (2) adversarial issue generation to provide misleading reproduction and error information while preserving the original issue semantics; and (3) iterative refinement of the adversarial issue statements based on the outputs of the APR agents. Empirical evaluation on three agent pipelines and five backend LLMs shows that SWExploit can produce patches that are both functionally correct and vulnerable (the attack success rate on the correct patch could reach 0.91, whereas the baseline ASRs are all below 0.20). Based on our evaluation, we are the first to challenge the traditional assumption that a patch passing all tests is inherently reliable and secure, highlighting critical limitations in the current evaluation paradigm for APR agents.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] BlueCodeAgent: A Blue Teaming Agent Powered by Automated Red Teaming for CodeGen AI
item.description: arXiv:2510.18131v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing research on CodeGen AI security mainly focuses on red teaming, which aims to uncover vulnerabilities and risks in AI-generated code. However, progress on the blue teaming side remains limited, as effective defenses require a deep security analysis of given tasks and edge cases. To fill in this gap, we propose BlueCodeAgent, an end-to-end blue teaming agent powered by automated red teaming. Our red teaming component generates diverse risky instances, providing effective edge cases and guidance for the subsequent blue teaming process. Our blue teaming agent then conducts multi-level defense, leveraging these red teaming examples to detect previously seen and unseen risk scenarios through constitution summarization and dynamic code analysis. Our evaluation across four representative code-related tasks (bias instruction detection, malicious instruction detection, vulnerable code detection, and prompt injection detection) shows that BlueCodeAgent achieves significant gains over diverse baselines. In particular, for vulnerability detection tasks, BlueCodeAgent integrates dynamic analysis to effectively reduce false positives, a challenging problem as base models tend to be over-conservative. Overall, with GPT-4o as the base model, BlueCodeAgent achieves an average F1 score improvement of 14.7% across four tasks compared to directly prompting the model, attributed to its ability to summarize actionable constitutions and perform dynamic analysis. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/1mocat/BlueCodeAgent.

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] When AI Joins the Team! A Model of How AI Adoption Relates To Social Patterns in Software Engineering Teams
item.description: arXiv:2608.03462v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Context: The growing adoption of AI-assisted development tools is changing how software teams collaborate, share knowledge, and coordinate, yet its consequences for team social dynamics remain largely unexplored. Gap: It is unclear whether AI adoption is associated with an increase or reduction in community smells,socio-technical anti-patterns reflecting coordination and communication breakdowns,and through which mechanisms. Method: Grounded in Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) theory, we validate instruments for HumanAI and HumanHuman interaction along two TMS dimensions, Specialization and Coordination, and test five PLS-SEM models on survey data from 152 software professionals using AI tools. Community smell constructs were derived from the literature and validated through expert surveys and factor analysis. Results: AI adoption relates to community smells not in a single way, but through mechanisms depending on the work. In specialization work, AI is associated with higher knowledge-sharing peer interaction, which is in turn associated with fewer smells. In coordination work, AI is directly associated with higher communication quality, complementing rather than replacing human interaction. Contributions: We provide an empirically validated, TMS-grounded model showing that the AIcommunity-smell relationship is contingent on the type of collaboration, with a reusable instrument and evidence-based implications for research and practice.

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] SWE-Bench ProMax: Benchmarking Agents on Large-Scale Multilingual Code Refactoring
item.description: arXiv:2608.09802v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As AI coding agents take on increasingly complex, long-horizon software engineering tasks, existing benchmarks are rapidly saturating and their evaluation quality has come under serious scrutiny: a recent audit found that nearly 60% of unsolved SWE-bench Verified instances contain flawed tests -- either overly narrow tests that reject correct solutions or overly broad tests that check unstated requirements -- and that frontier models can verbatim reproduce gold patches from training data. Code refactoring, which requires coordinated, behavior-preserving changes across many files, offers a substantially harder and more realistic test of agent capability, yet remains underserved by current benchmarks. We introduce SWE-Bench ProMax, an expert-curated, multilingual code refactoring benchmark of 170 instances drawn from real commits across seven programming languages (Python, Java, TypeScript, Go, C, C++, and Rust). Every instance undergoes rigorous, multi-stage curation that directly addresses the quality problems identified in prior benchmarks: issue descriptions are rewritten from scratch to provide precise, unambiguous specifications, and test suites are manually reviewed to remove overly narrow and overly broad tests. Tasks with insufficient complexity or limited cross-file scope are filtered out, yielding a benchmark of challenging, large-scale refactoring tasks that average 11.5 modified files and 261.6 lines of code per instance, substantially exceeding the scale of existing benchmarks. Experiments with frontier models under two agent scaffolds show that the best model achieves only 41.2% resolve rate, confirming that SWE-Bench ProMax presents a meaningful and unsaturated challenge for current AI coding agents. Our benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/swe-bench-promax/SWE-Bench-ProMax.

item.title: [arXiv-PL 2026] Countable Nondeterminism in Weighted Programming with an Application to Mechanized Foundations for Probabilistic Program Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.39723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weighted programming is a framework by Batz et al. for describing mathematical models or optimization problems as imperative programs parametrized over semirings and then analyzing them with program verification techniques like weakest precondition calculi. Applications include reasoning about expected outcomes of probabilistic programs and competitive analysis of online algorithms. We extend weighted programming with (1) countable nondeterminism and (2) user-defined additive rewards, where programs are parametrized over modules instead of semirings. The resulting framework enables reasoning about expected resource consumption of probabilistic programs and about optimal scores of combinatorial games. A technical challenge is that wp-calculi for weighted programs with (1) and (2) over arbitrary modules can be unsound, because it is well-known that continuity properties commonly used in program semantics break in the presence of countable nondeterminism. We study conditions under which a wp-style transformer for reasoning about weighted programs is sound with respect to an operational ground truth defined in terms of weighted decision processes (WDPs) - transition systems that generalize Markov decision processes by drawing transition weights and state rewards from a module. Based on those conditions, we show that a range of concrete instances of the weighted programming framework enjoy sound weakest precondition reasoning. We demonstrate the usefulness of our wp-semantics through case studies for different modules. We mechanized our extended weighted programming framework and our main soundness results in the interactive theorem prover Lean. Instantiating these results for probabilistic programming yields, to the best of our knowledge, the first mechanized proof of a fixed point characterization of minimal expected rewards in Markov decision processes with countable nondeterminism.
item.author: cs.PL updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-LG 2026] A Separation Principle for Adversarial Attacks and Defense of Graph Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.38127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adversarial attacks on graph neural networks (GNNs) have been studied as a model-centric optimization problem driven by gradients, learned policies, or meta-learning, with the graph treated as a passive substrate. This view overlooks a defining feature of GNNs: their predictions are produced by structured message passing along the graph, so their adversarial vulnerabilities are encoded as much in the geometry of the graph as in the learned weights. We develop a structure-driven framework for feature attacks in which the attack is derived from the spectral properties of the normalized adjacency operator. Its central result is a separation principle: under a natural relaxation of the attack objective, the optimal feature perturbation is rank one and factorizes into a graph-dependent component (degree-proportional spatial allocation, depending only on the graph) and a weight-dependent component (top singular vector of the composed weights, depending only on the weights). Node degree thus emerges as the fundamental graph quantity governing adversarial vulnerability to feature perturbations. The resulting attack, which we call SepAttack, requires no gradient computation, carries analytical guarantees, achieves competitive or superior performance against established baselines such as Nettack and IG-Attack with up to ${\sim}70\times$ speedup in the targeted setting, and transfers near-perfectly across architectures on continuous-feature graphs because its graph-dependent component is architecture-invariant by construction. We further derive a separation-principle adversarial training procedure (SepAT) directly from the closed-form worst-case attack and report robustness gains on binary-feature benchmarks.
item.author: cs.LG updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-LG 2026] CalibForge: Adversarial Solver Calibration for Scaling Learnable Terminal Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2608.06352v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Training terminal agents requires executable and verifiable tasks that are not merely solvable, but appropriately challenging for learning. Executable validation establishes feasibility, yet does not reveal how a task behaves relative to a given solver setting. In this paper, we present CalibForge, an autonomous terminal-task synthesis system that uses verified solver behavior to revise candidate tasks through adversarial solver calibration. Multi-solver calibration targets disagreement within a heterogeneous solver pool, whereas contrastive solver calibration targets a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation; both operationalize a solver-relative learnable zone anchored in demonstrated solvability. Using CalibForge, we construct 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks. Our ablations show that both strategies yield more effective supervision than authoring and validation alone or ordinary single-solver feedback. Models trained on the full collection achieve 31.84% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The largest improvements over the corresponding base model reach 23.97 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 26.54 points on SWE-bench Pro, and 30.04 points on Doc2Repo. Together, these results support solver-relative learnability as a practical target for constructing effective and transferable agent training data.

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] Silent and Costly: Characterizing and Detecting Prompt-Caching Mis-Integration in LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.34817v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) services process massive volumes of user requests, resulting in substantial inference costs. To reduce both cost and latency, providers have introduced prompt caching. However, correctly integrating prompt caching is non-trivial due to heterogeneous provider-specific APIs and continuously evolving caching semantics. To understand prompt-caching mis-integration in downstream applications, we conduct the first empirical study of 120 prompt-caching-related pull requests from 10 popular open-source agent systems. Our findings show that prompt-caching mis-integrations arise in both request-side misconfiguration and read-side usage miscount. More importantly, most mis-integrations fail silently without causing observable runtime failures. Motivated by these findings, we design CACHELINT, which models a prompt-caching mis-integration as an invocation site together with the preconditions required for correct cache integration. CACHELINT locates caching invocation sites with CodeQL and discharges each precondition either against a dated provider capability oracle or with an LLM guard check. CACHELINT achieves 0.71 precision and 0.78 recall in identifying the 120 labeled mis-integrations across the 10 studied agent systems. Our evaluation further demonstrates the effectiveness of CACHELINT in real-world settings, identifying 32 mis-integrations across 571 agent projects with 0.86 precision. These findings have received 21 developer confirmations and led to 18 upstream fixes, including one in Anthropic's official SDK.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] When AI Agrees Too Much: Manipulating Automated Code Review via Bias Injection
item.description: arXiv:2603.18740v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automated Code Review (ACR) systems integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in software development workflows, ranging from interactive assistants to autonomous agents in CI/CD pipelines. In this paper, we study how LLM-based vulnerability detection in ACR is affected by the framing effect: the tendency to let the presentation of information override its semantic content in forming judgments. We examine whether adversaries can exploit this through contextual-bias injection (crafting PR metadata to bias ACR security judgments) as a supply-chain attack vector against real-world ACR pipelines. To this end, we first conduct a large-scale exploratory study across 6 LLMs under five framing conditions, establishing the framing effect as a systematic and widespread phenomenon in LLM-based vulnerability detection. We then design a realistic and controlled experimental environment, evaluating 33 CVEs across 20 real-world projects and two popular ACR pipelines (Claude Code and CodeRabbit), to assess the susceptibility of real-world ACR pipelines to vulnerability re-introduction attacks. We employ two attack strategies: a template-based attack inspired by prior related work, and a novel LLM-assisted refinement attack. We find that template-based attacks are ineffective and may even backfire, as direct biasing attempts raise suspicions. Our refinement attack, on the other hand, is successful in 32/33 (97%) cases, exploiting a fundamental asymmetry: attackers can iteratively refine attacks against a local clone of the review pipeline, while defenders have only one chance to detect them. Overall, our findings highlight the dangers of over-relying on ACR and stress the importance of human oversight and contributor trust in the development process.

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] UnityBench-Mini3D: Evaluating LLM Agents for 3D Game Development in Unity
item.description: arXiv:2610.35980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Game development stresses coding agents in ways general software engineering does not: correctness depends on how engine APIs, serialized scene state, and runtime behavior interact, not on source code alone. Existing benchmarks mainly target platforms such as Godot and heavily rely on LLM judges or coarse task-level outcomes. We present UnityBench-Mini3D, a benchmark of 77 project-level Unity tasks organized around seven expert-defined skill categories rather than tutorials or genres, with three difficulty tiers. Each task pairs a complete Unity project with natural-language requirements and is evaluated using 1,178 held-out, human-authored milestone tests covering scene structure, component configuration, and runtime behavior. This in-engine evaluation provides deterministic partial credit, localizes failures, and distinguishes partial implementations from complete solutions without relying on subjective judges. Across 21 models and 9 coding harnesses, the average pass rate reaches 80.9% on easy tasks but falls to 35.2% on hard tasks, with just 57.7% overall. UnityBench-Mini3D provides a reproducible, diagnostic testbed distinguishing systems across difficulty levels.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] Generation and Verification: Human-Agent Collaboration for Safety-Critical Automotive Software Engineering
item.description: arXiv:2610.35982v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Research on coding agents mainly focuses on generation quality. Yet, safety-critical automotive software makes two additional demands. It prioritizes verification, since every change is reviewed, traced to a requirement, and checked against industry standards such as MISRA and AUTOSAR before it can be committed. It is also a narrow domain, written against layered architectures, embedded resource constraints, and organization-specific interface conventions that are scarce in the data general-purpose LLMs are trained on. We present a coding assistant for automotive C/C++ that addresses both demands. First, it exposes three tools to the user over the Model Context Protocol (generate, edit, and verify), allowing developers to run verify on any code on demand rather than relying on the agent to check its own output. Second, rather than using a general-purpose model, we customize the underlying LLM for the automotive domain through prompt engineering and fine-tuning. We construct a dataset from automotive production code of AUMOVIO, where each function is paired with the requirement texts and Unified Modeling Language (UML) behavior it must satisfy. In a two-week pilot on active production projects, developers report verify as the most-used tool and confirm using it on their own code and not only on generated output. Comparing model customization strategies, 75% prefer the faster prompt-engineered configuration. MISRA- and AUTOSAR-inspired pattern checkers indicate that prompt engineering achieves a lower number of violations on C, while fine-tuning shows better conformance with architecture patterns for C++.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] PROBE: Frontier Coding Agents Find Different Bugs Than Maintainers Fix
item.description: arXiv:2610.35987v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Proactive bug discovery is an important software-engineering problem. Even though coding agents are already widely deployed in this domain, their capabilities remain understudied. In particular, the challenging task of finding all bugs that human maintainers would repair across an entire repository has not been studied yet. To close this gap, we introduce PROBE, a benchmark consisting of all 2,457 bugs fixed over the course of 18 months across 20 diverse GitHub repositories, together with a method for matching candidate findings to this partial reference set. We evaluate coding agents across frontier models and find they all achieve a recall of below $21\%$ and a precision of less than $9\%$ with respect to the reference set. While stronger models increase recall substantially from $8\%$ to $17\%$, they do not improve precision. Surprisingly, despite the low precision, LLM and human evaluators still judge $85\%$ of findings valid. Crucially, we find that found bug distributions are similar across agents but differ substantially from those of bugs fixed by maintainers. The practical relevance of bug discovery and the low recall of frontier models make this benchmark a valuable resource for both model users and developers.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] CIVER: Causal Intervention Verification for Reliable Code Review
item.description: arXiv:2610.36010v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Code review is essential for maintaining software repositories by identifying defects, improving code quality, and supporting reliable software evolution. With the growing adoption of LLM-based coding agents, an increasing number of code contributions and repository changes are generated by these agents. Consequently, LLM-based code review agents are becoming increasingly prevalent to evaluate these contributions and maintain software quality. However, LLM reviewers often generate lengthy reviews containing numerous potential issues, many of which are false positives or lack sufficient evidence. These unreliable reviews can mislead developers and downstream coding agents, motivating the need to distinguish actionable findings from unsupported claims. We propose CIVER, a causal intervention-based framework that identifies the core issues underlying code-review findings and distinguishes genuine defects from false positives. CIVER integrates three modules: a review module assesses findings, an intervention module generates repair-oriented perturbations, and a verifier module scores review reliability. Through joint optimization via expert iteration, the three modules identify genuine defects by responding to targeted repairs while remaining stable under unrelated changes. Extensive experiments on SWE-Review-Bench demonstrate that CIVER correctly identifies 77% of genuine defects through targeted repairs. Cross-project and downstream repair evaluations further demonstrate that CIVER generalizes across repositories and improves coding agents' task success rates, highlighting its effectiveness for reliable automated code review.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] Benchmarking LLM Agents for Behaviorally Adequate Test Generation from Software Requirements
item.description: arXiv:2610.36584v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As large language model agents increasingly compile natural-language requirements into repository-level code, requirement-to-test generation grows in importance to provide validation constraints (or harness) to guide code generation. Yet it remains unclear whether current agents can generate tests that validate the required behavior when the implementation of that behavior is withheld. Existing test-generation benchmarks mostly focus on white-box testing, whereas the requirement--test-related study usually requires evaluation on semantic alignment between the given documents and the generated tests. We introduce Req2Test-Bench, a benchmark containing 5,086 execution-validated instances recovered from developer-authored behavior-driven development (BDD) artifacts in 8 open-source projects, spanning 5 programming languages and 4 BDD frameworks. Each instance pairs a natural-language requirement in Gherkin with its developer-written Test Implementation. Given the requirement, target interfaces of the required behavior, an agent must generate a complete, potentially multi-file Test Implementation. Evaluation of 8 agent--model--reasoning configurations reveals a substantial gap between execution success and behavioral adequacy, which is measured strictly as kill-completeness: a kill-complete test kills every mutant that the ground-truth test kills. The best-performing configuration, Codex with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, produces passing tests for 82.8% of instances, yet only 33.8% are behaviorally adequate. We find that (1) scaling up agents yields sharply diminishing returns in behavioral adequacy relative to generation cost; (2) under-specified requirements cause the information gap, including ambiguous setup and implicit expected outcomes; and (3) requirement-grounded harnesses that steer agent non-determinism offer a promising direction for improvement.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] Skill Dreaming: Evolving Repository Skills through Pull Request Streams
item.description: arXiv:2610.36188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on reusable skills for complex software engineering tasks, making skill libraries essential for repository development and maintenance. However, repository-specific skills must evolve with changing code structures, implementation conventions, and maintenance requirements. Pull requests (PRs) provide a natural source of such knowledge by recording how repositories evolve through implementation and review. Meanwhile, new PRs must follow repository-specific implementation patterns, modify related components consistently, and ensure that existing tests continue to pass while adding coverage for new functionality. This creates a mutually reinforcing cycle: PRs provide knowledge for updating skills, while these skills improve future PRs, maintain repositories, and support further skill evolution. To enable this co-evolution of PRs, repositories, and skills, we propose Skill Dreaming, a framework that learns from PR streams to guide continuous repository development and maintenance. Given a repository and its PR history, Skill Dreaming builds a repository-specific skill library by extracting executable knowledge from validated PRs and continuously refines the skills as new PR information becomes available. These skills guide coding agents not only in implementing requested features but also in maintaining associated tests, documentation, compatibility, and repository conventions. By integrating PR analysis, skill management, code execution, and continuous integration, Skill Dreaming provides an end-to-end workflow for applying learned skills to repository changes and incorporating subsequent PR outcomes into future skill updates.

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering?
item.description: arXiv:2603.15401v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agent skills, structured procedural knowledge packages injected at inference time, are increasingly used to augment LLM agents on software engineering tasks. However, their real utility in end-to-end development settings remains unclear, and no standard procedure tests an individual skill before installation. We present swe-skills-bench, a skill-centric, requirement-driven benchmark that measures how much individual agent skills improve performance on real-world software engineering (SWE) tasks. We start from 98 public SWE skills, each paired with a real GitHub repository pinned at a fixed commit. For each skill, we derive repository-specific requirements, create executable verifiers, and build a reproducible environment. Under each of four agent-model configurations, we run every task once without the skill and once with it, yielding 3,920 paired evaluations. For each requirement, we compute a paired delta, i.e., the change in outcome when the skill is added. We then aggregate these deltas across a skill's ten requirements into a per-skill utility profile, and use a statistical test to classify each skill as Golden (significantly helpful), Ineffective (no significant effect), or Harmful (significantly detrimental). Our results show that skills provide limited benefits: 92 of 98 skills have no statistically significant effect, and adding skills raises the average pass ratio only from 76.6% to 76.9%. The few helpful skills supply procedures that the agent would otherwise omit (gains of up to $+17.7$ points). In contrast, harmful skills anchor the agent on their own templates and override the task's explicit instructions (losses of up to -17.0 points). Our code is available at https://github.com/ControllableModel/SWE-Skills-Bench.
